# Designing an On-Call Rotation for a Six-Person Engineering Team

Designing an effective on-call rotation for a six-person team requires balancing operational coverage with sustainable workloads to prevent engineer burnout. Proper scheduling, clear handoffs, and transparent compensation policies form the foundation of a healthy rotation [9].

## Standard Scheduling Models

For a six-person engineering team, the most common and practical model is a weekly rotation [1]. In a six-person pool, engineers can cycle through primary and secondary tiers (offset by three positions), meaning each person spends one week on primary and one week on secondary in a six-week cycle [2]. Alternatively, teams can use a primary-only model where each person is on call roughly once a month, which is frequent enough to keep tooling familiar but infrequent enough to prevent burnout [6]. Schedules should be published at least 4 to 6 weeks in advance [1], and bookable absences must be entered at least 2 weeks ahead [2]. 

## Preventing Burnout and Managing Fatigue

To protect team members from burnout, teams must distribute on-call duties equally and make shift-switching simple [4]. Juggling daily workloads alongside on-call duties causes fatigue; therefore, workflows should be created that are less reliant on on-call engineers during the day, and on-call weeks should carry a reduced sprint commitment [2][5]. Teams should cut alert volume, protect development time, document everything needed at 3 AM, and structure shifts to a maximum of 12 hours (or 8 hours for heavy page loads) to minimize error rates [4][6].

## Compensation and Alert Threshold Policies

Employers must review their on-call policies for compliance with federal and state regulations regarding compensable time and waiting time, as regulatory scrutiny and salary thresholds for overtime exemptions continue to rise [8]. NO EVIDENCE AVAILABLE for specific internal alert threshold dollar amounts, but best practices dictate establishing multi-layer escalation paths and cutting alert volume to avoid alert fatigue [4][9]. Escalation paths should never dead-end [9]; a standard path might page the primary instantly, escalate to the secondary after 5 minutes, and reach out to the engineering manager or CTO at 15 minutes [2][3].

## Handoffs and Documentation

Handoffs should be written, public, posted in the team channel rather than sent via direct message, and kept short (around two minutes) so they are never skipped [2][10]. A proper handoff covers six items: open incidents with current status, self-resolved watch items, known noise with an expiry date, incoming changes, suppressed or overridden alerts, and any critical context [2]. Additionally, teams must document common fixes in a runbook so incoming responders do not start from scratch [3].

## Conclusion

A successful six-person on-call rotation relies on predictable weekly scheduling, fair distribution of labor, and a reduced daytime workload during on-call weeks [1][2][5]. By enforcing concise written handoffs, maintaining runbooks, and complying with labor regulations regarding compensable time, teams can build a sustainable, low-friction incident response process [2][3][8][9].

At the end of an on-call shift, it’s a good practice to have some kind of formal handoff. This can take the form of a team meeting, where the outgoing on-call responder summarizes the incidents for their shift. It can also take the form of an email, shared document, or saved query in your incident response platform that highlights the current and recent alerts and how they were handled, if they are closed, or the current status for those ongoing into the next shift. [...] The purpose of the handoff is to make sure the incoming on-call responder has all of the information and context for the current state of the environment.
